summary:
Imo State stands fully inside Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies throughout the country and reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. Sharia criminal law, under which male sodomy carries the death penalty, applies in twelve northern states and does not apply in Imo, which is a southern state.

Police enforcement against same-sex gatherings in Imo is active and recent. On 19 February 2025 the Imo Police Command announced that it had foiled a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arrested eight suspects and charged them under the anti-homosexuality law with its 14-year term, while attendees who fled were placed on a police search list. The command described the operation as covering a gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act, so gender expression is drawn into the same charge and same sentence.

Community vigilantism runs alongside police action. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them. A follow-up NoStringsNG inquiry found that the two victims were themselves taken into custody by police and may need legal support, so an accusation of same-sex conduct produced both mob violence and arrest.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Trans-specific violence is documented nationally with no prosecution to date. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Extraction and violence by police are reported well beyond Imo. TimesLIVE (March 2025) describes Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, who was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text, and the same statute and the same police culture apply in Imo.

The pattern of enforcement in Imo in 2025 sits inside a wider national posture in which the SSMPA operates alongside colonial-era provisions and, in twelve states, Sharia Zina law carrying corporal and capital penalties. A visitor crossing state lines inside Nigeria moves between enforcement regimes that differ in severity but not in direction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Imo accused of same-sex conduct face prosecution under a national statute with no state-level discretion over whether charges are brought, and no local protection mechanism documented in these sources. The 2018 Isiala Mbano case shows that the same accusation can trigger mob violence, public stripping and police custody at once, with the NoStringsNG inquiry recording that the two men may need legal support.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Residents live with the knowledge that a public allegation of same-sex conduct or visibly non-conforming gender presentation can attract both official processing and collective punishment, and that no hate-crime statute, anti-discrimination law or relationship recognition provides a counterweight.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources available here do not address entry and visa screening for trans visitors into Nigeria, rules on gender markers in passports or other travel documents, airport or border treatment of visibly trans arrivals, bathroom and facilities access, access to hormone therapy or other gender-affirming care, or recognition of marriages and partnerships concluded abroad. Nothing in the inventory resolves these questions for Imo.

The outcome of the February 2025 Owerri West prosecutions is unresolved: the police command announced arrests and charges, and these sources do not record convictions, sentences or release of the eight suspects, nor the disposition of the attendees placed on a search list.

The fate of the two men taken into custody after the April 2018 Isiala Mbano assault is unresolved; the sources record their arrest and a possible need for legal support but no prosecution outcome or remedy.

Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted into law remains unsettled by these sources, as does any state-level legislation specific to Imo on hate crimes, discrimination or gender recognition.
